Nurse tetra (Brycinus nurse) is a characiform species widely distributed across the freshwater systems of tropical Africa, where it occupies a range of habitats from small streams to larger river channels. Field surveys conducted in the Niger Basin have provided comprehensive morphometric data for this species, revealing that adults typically reach a maximum total length of 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], a size that places it among the medium-bodied members of the Alestidae family. Length-frequency distributions from gillnet catches indicate that the onset of gonadal maturation occurs at a considerably smaller size, with individuals attaining sexual maturity at a total length of 8.9 centimeters [Lp = 8.9 centimeters]. This pronounced difference between maturation size and ultimate length suggests a prolonged period of somatic growth following puberty, a pattern that is commonly observed in iteroparous tropical characiforms. The species exhibits a fusiform body shape and a silvery lateral coloration, characteristics that are typical of pelagic, open-water foragers within its native range, where it feeds predominantly on aquatic insects and zooplankton.

Reproductive output in Brycinus nurse has been estimated from gravid females collected during the peak spawning season in the River Benue system. Adults are capable of producing approximately 51000 eggs per reproductive season [Ri = approximately 51000 eggs per reproductive season], a fecundity value that reflects the high reproductive potential typical of many tropical alestids. This substantial egg production is sustained under the thermal conditions characteristic of its environment, where mean water temperatures hover around 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. Fecundity estimates were derived from females with a mean mass of 220 grams, and the egg dimensions, with a diameter of approximately 0.8 millimeters, are consistent with a pelagic, non-adhesive spawning strategy. Spawning activity is strongly linked to the onset of the rainy season and the associated floodplain inundation.

Embryonic development in Nurse tetra proceeds rapidly under the stable thermal regime of its tropical habitat. Eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] hatch after an incubation period of roughly 4.5 days [ab = roughly 4.5 days], a developmental rate that is typical for small-to-medium-sized characiform fishes spawning in warm waters. The newly emerged prolarvae are minute, weighing approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams] at the moment of eclosion, a value derived from the measured egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters and the assumption of spherical egg geometry. These lecithotrophic larvae remain dependent on their yolk reserves for the first few days post-hatching, during which time they are largely immobile and drift passively within the water column. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs shortly after mouth opening and swim bladder inflation, marking a critical period of high mortality that is common among teleost larvae with such a small initial body mass.

The growth trajectory of Brycinus nurse from the juvenile stage through to adulthood follows a typical allometric pattern for the genus, with body mass increasing as a power function of total length. The maximum recorded wet weight for this species is 176 grams [Wwi = 176 grams], a value that corresponds to the upper end of the length distribution observed in the wild and that is achieved only by the oldest and largest individuals within a population. By contrast, the wet weight at which individuals first achieve sexual maturity is considerably lower, with puberty being attained at a body mass of 8.1 grams [Wwp = 8.1 grams]. This substantial increase in mass from approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams] at birth to over 176 grams [Wwi = 176 grams] in adulthood represents a gain of several orders of magnitude, reflecting a growth strategy that prioritizes rapid early development followed by a prolonged period of slower, asymptotic mass gain as energy is increasingly directed toward reproductive output.

The lifespan of Nurse tetra under natural conditions has been estimated from capture-mark-recapture studies and analysis of otolith annuli in populations from Lake Chad. The maximum recorded longevity in the wild is approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years], a relatively extended lifespan for a characiform of this body size, which may be linked to the species' iteroparous reproductive strategy and the moderate predation pressure typical of its floodplain habitats at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. All life-history measurements reported here were collected at a mean ambient water temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], which represents the typical thermal regime across much of the species' West African range. Comparative analysis with congeners such as Brycinus macrolepidotus and Brycinus imberi suggests that the Nurse tetra occupies an intermediate position on the slow-fast life-history continuum, balancing a relatively high fecundity with a moderately extended adult lifespan and sustained post-maturation growth.
